title: The Story of Sir Gawaine: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Got Lost in the Forest, and How He Met with a Very Strange Adventure in a Castle He Came To._

Some time after this, King Arthur was at Tintagalon on certain business of state. Queen Guinevere and her Court, together with the King’s Court, traveled from Camelot to Carleon. There they stayed until the King should finish his business at Tintagalon and join them.

It was springtime, and everything felt bright and cheerful, so King Arthur was seized by a great longing for adventure. He called a favorite esquire named Boisenard and said, “Boisenard, this day is so pleasant that I can hardly hold myself still for the joy of it. My heart feels ready to burst with wanting something. So I am of a mind to go wandering about the countryside, with only you for company.”
Boisenard answered, “My lord, I know of nothing that would please me more.”
King Arthur said, “Very well. Let us leave this place so that no one knows we have gone. We will ride to Carleon and surprise the Queen by arriving when she does not expect us.”
So Boisenard fetched armor that carried no coat of arms and dressed the King in it. Then the two of them rode out together, and no one knew that they had left the castle.

When they reached the open fields, King Arthur whistled and sang and joked and laughed and made merry. He was like a war-horse let loose on the grass, which loves the sunshine and the warm air and becomes a colt again.

After a while they came to the forest and rode on in great content. They took this path and then that path, for no reason except that the day was so bright and cheerful. Before long they had lost their way in the tangle of the woods and did not know where they were.

Finding themselves lost, they rode more carefully, trying first one way and then another. But they could not find their way out of the tangle. Night fell, and they still did not know where they were. Everything grew dark and gloomy, and the woods all around them were full of strange and unfamiliar sounds.
Then King Arthur said, “Boisenard, this is a very puzzling situation, and I do not know how we will find a place to sleep tonight.”
Boisenard said, “My lord, if you give me leave, I will climb one of these trees and see whether I can spot any sign of a home in this wilderness.” King Arthur said, “Do so, I ask you.”
So Boisenard climbed a very tall tree, and from the top he saw a light a long way off. He said, “My lord, I see a light in that direction.” Then he climbed down from the tree again.

King Arthur and Boisenard rode toward the place where Boisenard had seen the light. Soon they came out of the forest into an open place, where they saw a huge castle with several tall towers. It looked grim and forbidding. The light Boisenard had seen came from this castle. The two rode up to it, and Boisenard shouted and pounded on the castle gate. At once a porter came and asked what they wanted. Boisenard said to him, “Fellow, we want to come in and stay tonight, for we are weary.” The porter asked, “Who are you?”—speaking roughly and rudely, for in the darkness he could not tell what sort of men they were. Then Boisenard said, “This is a knight of very high rank, and I am his esquire. We have lost our way in the forest, and now we have come here looking for shelter.”
“Sir,” said the porter, “if you know what is good for you, you will sleep in the forest rather than come into this place. This is no good shelter for wandering knights.”
At this King Arthur spoke to the porter, for what the porter had said made him very curious. He said, “No, we will not go away. We demand to stay here tonight.”
Then the porter said, “Very well, you may come in.” He opened the gate, and they rode into the courtyard of the castle.

At the noise of their arrival, many lights appeared inside the castle, and a number of servants came running out. Some helped King Arthur and Boisenard to get down from their horses, and others led the horses away. Still others brought basins of water for them to wash in. When they had washed their faces and hands, other servants led them into the castle.

As they entered, they heard a great noise of many people talking and laughing together, mixed with the sound of singing and harp music. They came into the great hall and saw that it was lit by a great number of candles and tapers and torches. A crowd of people sat at a table spread for a feast. At the head of the table sat a knight who was well along in years, with hair and beard as white as milk. Yet he was very strong and sturdy, with wonderfully broad shoulders and a deep chest. He looked stern and forbidding. He was dressed completely in black, and around his neck he wore a gold chain with a gold locket hanging from it.

When this knight saw King Arthur and Boisenard come into the hall, he called out to them in a booming voice and told them to come and sit with him at the head of the table. They did so, and those sitting there made room for them, so that they sat beside the knight.

King Arthur and Boisenard were very hungry, so they ate eagerly and enjoyed the entertainment they were given. All the while the knight kept them company with pleasant talk, speaking of whatever would amuse them most. After a while the feast ended, and they stopped eating.

Then, all of a sudden, the knight said to King Arthur, “Messire, you are young and high-spirited, and I do not doubt that you have a great heart. What do you say to a little sport between the two of us?” King Arthur looked at the knight very steadily. He thought the man’s face was not as old as it seemed, for his eyes were very bright and shone like sparks of light. So he was doubtful, and he said, “Sir, what sport do you have in mind?” At this the knight burst into laughter and said, “It is a very strange sport. You and I will test each other to see how much courage each of us has.” King Arthur asked, “How will we test that?” The knight answered, “This is what we will do. You and I will stand in the middle of this hall, and you will have leave to try to cut off my head. If I can take that blow without dying of it, then I will have leave to cut off your head in the same way.”
At these words King Arthur felt great dread, and he said, “That is very strange sport for two men to take part in.”

When King Arthur said this, everyone in the hall burst out laughing, and they laughed as though they would never stop. When they had grown a little quieter, the knight of the castle said, “Sir, are you afraid of that sport?” King Arthur grew angry and said, “No, I am not afraid. No man has ever had reason to say that I showed fear of anyone.” “Very well,” said the knight of the castle. “Then let us try the sport I spoke of.” And King Arthur said, “I am willing.”

Then Boisenard came to King Arthur where he stood and said, “My lord, do not agree to this. Let me take on this challenge in your place, for I am sure that some great treachery is planned against you.” But King Arthur said, “No. No man will take my danger upon himself. I will face my own danger without asking anyone else to bear it.” Then he said to the knight of the castle, “Sir, I am ready for the sport you spoke of. But who is to strike the first blow, and how shall we draw lots for it?” “Messire,” said the knight of the castle, “we will draw no lots. Since you are the guest in this place, you will have the first try at this sport.”

With that, the knight stood up and took off his black robe. Underneath he wore a shirt of fine linen, very skillfully worked, and red hose. Then he opened the linen shirt at the throat and turned the collar down, to leave his neck bare for the blow. He said, “Now, Sir Knight, you will have to strike well if you want to win at this sport.”

But King Arthur showed no fear of the task. He stood up and drew Excalibur, so that the blade flashed with dazzling brightness. Then he measured his distance, raised the sword, and struck the knight of the castle on the neck with all his might. And behold! The blade cut through the knight’s neck with wonderful ease, and the head flew from the body and landed far away.

But the knight’s body did not fall. Instead it stood up and walked to where the head lay. The hands of the body picked up the head and set it back on the shoulders, and behold! The knight was as sound and whole as he had ever been in his life.

At this all the people in the castle shouted and made great merriment. They told King Arthur that it was now his turn to try the sport. So the King got ready, taking off his surcoat and opening his shirt at the throat, as the knight of the castle had done. Boisenard cried out in great sorrow. Then the knight of the castle said, “Sir, are you afraid?” King Arthur said, “No, I am not afraid. Every man must die some time, and it seems that my time has now come. I am to give up my life in this foolish way, through no fault of my own.”
Then the knight of the castle said, “Well, stand back a little way, so that I do not strike you too close and so spoil the power of my blow.”

So King Arthur stood in the middle of the hall, and the knight of the castle swung his sword several times without striking. Several times he also laid the blade on King Arthur’s neck, and it was very cold. Then King Arthur cried out in great anger, “Sir, it is your right to strike, but I beg you not to torment me like this.” “No,” said the knight of the castle. “It is my right to strike when it pleases me, and I will not strike before then. If it pleases me, I will torment you for a long while before I kill you.” So he laid his sword on King Arthur’s neck several more times, and King Arthur said no more but bore the torment with a very steady spirit.

Then the knight of the castle said, “You seem to be a very brave and honorable knight, and I have a mind to make an agreement with you.” King Arthur asked, “What is that agreement?” “It is this,” said the knight of the castle. “I will spare your life for a year and a day, if you will give me your knightly word to return here at the end of that time.”
King Arthur answered, “Very well, I agree.” He promised on his knightly honor that he would come back when the year was over, and he swore this oath upon the cross-shaped hilt of Excalibur.

Then the knight of the castle said, “I will make another agreement with you.” “What is it?” said King Arthur. “My second agreement is this,” said the knight of the castle. “I will give you a riddle. If you can answer it when you return here, and make no mistake in your answer, then I will spare your life and set you free.” King Arthur asked, “What is the riddle?” The knight answered, “The riddle is this: What is it that a woman wants most of all in the world?”

“Sir,” said King Arthur, “I will try to find the answer to that riddle, and I thank you for sparing my life for so long and for giving me a chance to escape my death.” At this the knight of the castle smiled a very sour smile and said, “I do not offer this out of mercy toward you, but because I take pleasure in tormenting you. What joy can you have in living your life when you know you must surely die at the end of one short year? And what pleasure can you have even in that year, when you will be tormented by worry to find the answer to my riddle?”
Then King Arthur said, “I think you are very cruel.” And the knight said, “I do not deny it.”

So that night King Arthur and Boisenard slept at the castle, and the next day they went on their way. King Arthur was heavy at heart and troubled. Even so, he ordered Boisenard to say nothing of what had happened and to keep it secret. Boisenard did as the King commanded and said nothing about that adventure.

In the year that followed, King Arthur put his affairs in order. He also searched everywhere for the answer to the riddle. Many people gave him plenty of answers. One said that a woman most wanted wealth, and another said beauty. One said she wanted the power to please, and another said she most wanted fine clothes. One said this and another said that, but none of the answers seemed to King Arthur good or right for his purpose.

So the year went by until only two weeks remained. Then King Arthur could not bear to stay where he was any longer, for it seemed to him that his time was very near. He was filled with bitter anxiety, and he was restless to be gone.
So he called Boisenard to him and said, “Boisenard, help me put on my armor, for I am going away.”
Then Boisenard burst into tears and said, “My lord, do not go.”

At this King Arthur looked sternly at his esquire and said, “Boisenard, what is this? Would you tempt me to break my honor? It is not very hard to die, but it would be very bitter to live my life in dishonor. So tempt me no more, but do as I order and keep quiet. And if I do not return within a month from now, then you may tell everything that has happened. You may tell Sir Constantine of Cornwall that he is to search the papers in my cabinet, and there he will find everything that must be done if death should overtake me.”

So Boisenard put a plain suit of armor on King Arthur, though he could hardly see what he was doing for the tears streaming from his eyes. He fastened a surcoat with no coat of arms over the King’s armor and gave the King a shield with no device. Then King Arthur rode away without thinking where the road led him. Of everyone he met he asked what it was that a woman most wanted, and no one could give him an answer that seemed to be the right one. So he was in great doubt and anguish of spirit.

The day before King Arthur was to keep his promise at that castle, he was wandering through the nearby forest, deeply troubled in spirit, because he did not know what he could do to save his life. As he wandered, he suddenly came upon a small hut built beneath a spreading oak tree. The tree and the hut were so tangled together that it was hard to tell where one ended and the other began. Many large, mossy rocks lay all around it, and the King might easily have walked past the hut. But he saw smoke rising from it, as from a fire burning inside. So he went to the hut, opened the door, and stepped in. At first he thought no one was there. Then he looked again and saw an old woman sitting hunched over a small fire on the hearth. King Arthur had never seen such an ugly old hag as the one bending over that fire. Her ears were huge and flapped about, and her hair hung down around her head like snakes. Her face was so covered in wrinkles that there was not a single spot without one. Her eyes were watery and clouded over, and her eyelids were red, as if she were always weeping. She had only one tooth in her mouth, and the hands she held out to the fire were like claws of bone.
Then King Arthur greeted her, and she greeted him in return. She said to him, “My lord King, where do you come from? And why have you come to this place?”

King Arthur was greatly astonished that the old woman knew who he was. He said, “Who are you, that you seem to know me?” “That does not matter,” she said. “I am someone who wishes you well. So tell me what trouble has brought you here at this time.” So the King told the old woman all his trouble, and he asked her if she knew the answer to the riddle, “What is it that a woman most desires?” “Yes,” said the old woman, “I know the answer to that riddle very well. But I will not tell it to you unless you promise me something in return.”

At this King Arthur was filled with great joy that the old woman knew the answer to the riddle. But he was also full of doubt about what she would ask of him. So he said, “What must you have in return for that answer?”
Then the old woman said, “If I help you guess your riddle correctly, you must promise that I will become the wife of one of the knights of your Court. I will choose him when you return home again.”

“Ha!” said King Arthur. “How can I promise that on behalf of anyone else?” Then the old woman said, “Are the knights of your Court not noble enough to do that to save you from death?” “I believe they are,” said King Arthur. With that he thought for a long while, saying to himself, “What will my kingdom do if I die now? I have no right to die.” So he said to the old woman, “Very well, I will make that promise.”
The old woman spoke to the King again. “Here is the answer to your riddle: a woman most wants to have her own way.” King Arthur felt sure the answer was right.

Then the old woman said, “My lord King, you have been tricked by the knight who led you into this trouble. He is a great conjurer and a very wicked magician. He carries his life not in his body, but in a crystal globe that he wears in a locket hanging around his neck. That is why, when you cut the head from his body, his life stayed in the locket and he did not die. If you had destroyed that locket, he would have died at once.”
“I will remember that,” said King Arthur.

So King Arthur stayed with the old woman that night, and she refreshed him with food and drink and looked after him very well. The next morning he set out for the castle where he had made his promise, and his heart was more cheerful than it had been for a whole year.
